keyVerseText: He shall pour the water out of his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters, and his king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted.
rootMeaning: The root of אֲגַג (ʼĂgag) is uncertain, though it may relate to the Hebrew word אָגֵא (ʼÂgêʼ), meaning "I shall increase," or possibly to a term meaning "flame." This suggests a connotation of elevation or intensity, which aligns with the lexicon's note that Agag means "I will overtop." Such imagery of rising or surpassing heightens the significance of the name beyond a mere proper noun, hinting at power or prominence.
usageInScripture: The term אֲגַג appears eight times in Scripture, consistently as a proper name for the Amalekite king, emphasizing his royal and symbolic status. Translations predominantly render it as "Agag" or "And Agag," reflecting its function as a title rather than a common noun. Its use in Numbers 24:7 as a symbol of might, where a king is said to be "higher than Agag," reveals its role as a benchmark for power and authority within the biblical narrative.
theologicalSignificance: Agag embodies the persistent opposition to God's people, representing the Amalekites who were enemies of Israel. The meaning "I will overtop" underscores the arrogance and defiance that stand against God's sovereign rule. Recognizing Agag as a symbol of worldly opposition invites believers to trust in God's ultimate supremacy over all earthly powers. The narrative of Saul sparing Agag but Samuel executing judgment foreshadows the necessity of obedience to God's commands and the consequences of compromise. This serves as a reminder of Christ's victory over sin and evil, affirming that no earthly king or power can surpass the kingdom of God.
keyVerseReflection: Numbers 24:7 declares, "His king shall be higher than Agag, and his kingdom shall be exalted," using Agag as a symbol of elevated power. The name here conveys a standard of might and prominence that the king surpasses, emphasizing divine exaltation. This imagery enriches our understanding of God's blessing and the supremacy of His chosen rulers, pointing forward to the ultimate reign of Christ, who is exalted far above all earthly authorities.
